newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Now Zaire's rebels start clean-up of diamond trade.
newsitem.headline: Now Zaire's rebels start clean-up of diamond trade.

text.p: Rebels controlled many of Zaire's diamond-producing areas on Monday after capturing the diamond centre of Mbuji-Mayi, and were already collecting revenue from sales worth well over $500 million a year.
Laurent Kabila's rebels promise a complete clean-up of the notoriously corrupt diamond sector, dominated until now by President Mobutu Sese Seko, his family and his generals.
The reforms are being tested in Kisangani, captured by the rebels on March 15 and which accounts for about 10 percent of Zaire's annual official trade in artisanal diamonds.

"Before, all the money went straight into pockets. Now people are happy because it will go into the public coffers and they will not be harassed by corrupt officials," said Yagi Sitolo, the new governor in Kisangani.
None of the affluence associated with diamonds has rubbed off on this dirty and dilapidated city of 500,000 people.
America Mineral Fields (AMF), a Canadian-registered mining company, is first off the blocks in a minor stampede for access to the vast mineral resources in a post-Mobutu era.

"I firmly believe Kabila is going to make a better Zaire without corruption. So far, everything they've said they'll do, they do," Joseph Martin, an AMF director, told Reuters in Kisangani, saying the company's real goal was exploration for copper, cobalt and other metals in southern Shaba province.

Last Friday AMF opened the first and so far only diamond buying office in the city to be licensed by the rebels. After 24 hours, Martin and his British buyers had spent $100,000 in cash on the mainly industrial stones brought by middlemen.
As sign-writers painted the office with the name "American Diamond Buyers", a small mob of middlemen milled outside discussing the new order. All their normal outlets are shut.
Before the rebels took over, Kisangani had about 60 diamond offices run by Lebanese traders and the main one run by Sediza, the De Beers subsidiary in Zaire.
Industry sources said most Lebanese-run offices were partnerships with members of Mobutu's elite and some diamonds were bought above the world price to launder dirty dollars.
The middlemen or "negociants" are suffering from the change since AMF buyers offer less money, saying they are in line with the price in Antwerp, centre of the world diamond trade.
"What I have here is unadulterated shit," one buyer snapped as he sifted the contents of a folded piece of paper. After some haggling, he accepted a price far below what he wanted.
The true value of Zaire's diamond business is a mystery because an unknown percentage of gems and industrial stones were smuggled out without any record or tax.

But officially, according to Belgian businessman Charles Thys, the annual trade was worth about $360 million for artisanally dug diamonds and $80 million for the production at the country's only modern mine, MIBA (Miniere de Bakwanga) at Mbuji-Mayi, a far bigger diamond centre than Kisangani.

The rebels captured Mbuji-Mayi and MIBA at the weekend and are setting their sights on Tshikapa, 300 km (185 miles) to the west and the home of the country's finest stones. That would leave Kabila in control of the business apart from the trade near the Angolan border.

Lando Batibuka of Kabila's finance ministry, who is supervising AMF and other offices likely to open soon, told Reuters: "The principle is that everyone in the business must eat," compared with the previous anarchy and corruption.
The rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) has started by slashing the cost of an annual licence for an exporter's buying office to $25,000.

Under Mobutu it was $150,000 but the money never reached the state treasury, Lando said. AMF's Martin said his company had already paid the $25,000. Exporters will pay a tax of 2.5 percent on their purchases to the rebels' central government.

Lando said negociants would pay taxes to regional authorities and diggers would be taxed at a lower level. Those two rates had yet to be announced but the system would ensure the profits of diamonds were fairly shared, he said.

The Alliance is cutting out the former fourth link in the chain, "commissionaires". Their rather superfluous activity was to tell negociants which buying office was paying the best price for their type of stones.
Diggers and middlemen must be nationals in future but licensed foreigners will be allowed to work as buyer-exporters.
The remaining Lebanese in Kisangani, whose former role in the diamond trade is viewed with distaste by Alliance officials, are watching the changes with concern.
They are hampered because their head offices are in the government-held capital Kinshasa. "Mobutu will not allow us to operate on both sides," one trader told Reuters.
